Article Title: Rashtrapati Bhavan hints at Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman's visit, retracts
Article Text:
India, Bangladesh in talks over PM Tarique Rahman’s Delhi visit; dates yet to be finalised amid extradition and bilateral issues

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India and Bangladesh remain in talks about PM Tarique Rahman's Delhi visit but the dates aren't locked in, diplomatic sources said on Friday. They denied Rahman would travel to India in the next few days after a Rashtrapati Bhavan release seemed to indicate otherwise.The press release, which said that the change of guard ceremony at Rashtrapati Bhavan forecourt would not take place on Saturday due to the full rehearsal for "the ceremonial welcome of the PM of Bangladesh", was later withdrawn. Amid confusion, the MEA said it had no update on the issue.Rahman's press secretary A A M Saleh said there was no decision yet on the PM's visit, reiterating that Dhaka awaited India's response on extradition of ex-PM Sheikh Hasina and other "fugitive criminals".However, a visit by Tarique Rahman in early Sept is not ruled out. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has invited Rahman for a bilateral visit and also to participate in the Brics summit in Sept as Bimstec chair.According to Dhaka, talks to finalise dates for the summit this month were vitiated by Sheikh Hasina’s Aug 5 virtual news conference.Dhaka now seems to have hardened its position on the issue, linking the visit to an explicit commitment it expects from India on Hasina’s extradition proceedings.Bangladesh also expects India to address its concerns on issues such as border killings and water sharing, including the 1996 Ganges Water Sharing Treaty, which governs dry-season water allocation, and expires late 2026.“As you would be aware, the Ganga Water Treaty was signed in 1996 for a period of 30 years. All river-related issues between India and Bangladesh are discussed under the Joint Rivers Commission. Further, meetings of the joint committee under the Ganga Water Treaty continue to be held at the technical level,” said MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, asked about JDU functionary Sanjay Jha’s statement that the treaty was not in Bihar’s interest.
Article Summary: India, bangladesh in talks over pm tarique rahman’s delhi visit; dates yet to be finalised amid extradition and bilateral issues. Prime minister narendra modi has invited rahman for a bilateral visit and also to participate in the brics summit in sept as bimstec chair.

The Federation of Seafarers and Indian Seafarers Union (FSUI) has released an old video showing a vessel carrying 22 crew members, including 21 Indians, coming under attack in the Strait of Hormuz on April 22.The footage shows several small boats surrounding the vessel, an RPG being fired and seafarers rushing to the ship’s alleyways to take cover as the confrontation unfolded.The union also released images showing crew members taking cover while the vessel was under attack.“These were not pirates. They were naval forces of the IRGC,” the FSUI said in a post on X.The union added that the footage highlighted the risks faced by seafarers in the Strait of Hormuz, arguing that advisories and guidelines alone could not ensure their safety.“Innocent seafarers need the assured presence of naval forces to truly protect them,” the FSUI said.The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) recently said 166 Indian seafarers remained in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz region, including 125 aboard six Indian-flagged vessels and 41 working on foreign-flagged ships.In an update on August 4, the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways said 3,972 Indian seafarers had been repatriated from the Gulf region, highlighting the scale of the effort to bring them out of the conflict zone.India is the world’s second-largest supplier of seafarers after the Philippines, with 311,936 personnel accounting for 12.16 per cent of the global maritime workforce, according to the BIMCO-ICS Seafarer Workforce Report 2026. Indian officers account for 13.41 per cent of the global officer workforce, while 171,218 Indian ratings make up 11.29 per cent of the global ratings workforce.The large presence of Indian seafarers in the region has also resulted in casualties since the Iran war began. Last month, the MEA said Indian seafarers had recorded the highest number of fatalities among all nationalities in attacks on commercial shipping.The government later informed Parliament that 10 Indian seafarers were among the 16 Indian nationals killed in the Middle East conflict.
Article Summary: Seafarers take cover as small boats surround vessel in hormuz. Video shows crew members taking cover while the vessel was under attack. “these were not pirates. They were naval forces of the irgc,” the fsui said.

Article Title: 'We fought wars with Pakistan too, but China will be India's main competitor': Ex-Army chief
Article Text:
General MM Naravane (Retd) on China and Pakistan

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Former Army chief General MM Naravane (Retired) on Thursday described China as India's "main competitor" in the years ahead, despite India having fought wars with both China and Pakistan."Pakistan and China are a totally different ballgame. We have fought wars with both of them. We have unsettled borders. So they will always remain on our radar as a threat, as a challenge," PTI quoted Naravane as saying at a book launch event in New Delhi.However, he distinguished between the two, saying India's immediate focus on Pakistan was driven largely by the continuing threat of terrorism, while describing China as a "competitor" rather than an "enemy." He emphasised that he had "purposely" used the term "competitor" for China."We have fought major wars with Pakistan, and because of their continued support to terrorism, our attention is towards our western borders. But I think we are very clear that in the long term and in the years to come, China is going to be our main competitor. And I purposely use the word competitor and not enemy," Naravane said.Naravane, who was Chief of Army Staff during the 2020 Ladakh clashes with China and led India's response, further stated that the two countries would be competitors across multiple domains, including politics, economics, trade and military affairs."They are going to be our main competitor in all fields. Political, economic, trade, and of course military also. And wherever there is competition, there is always a little bit of conflict," the retired Army general observed.He emphasised that India should seek to manage such differences through dialogue and diplomatic mechanisms rather than resorting to force."It is up to us to try to resolve those conflicts, those differences, through the mechanisms of talks, dialogues. And taking recourse to the use of force should always be the last priority," he said.However, he also stressed that India must maintain credible military preparedness to deter any potential misadventure."There comes a moment when you realise that this is not going to happen. And therefore, you have to have a strong deterrence. That is why the armed forces have to be ready at all times. You have to have a strong deterrence to stop anybody from taking recourse to the use of force or any misadventure," he remarked.
Article Summary: General mm naravane (retd) on china and pakistan: "pakistan and china are a totally different ballgame" he emphasised that he had "purposely" used the term "competitor" for china.naravane was chief of army staff during the 2020 ladakh clashes with china.

Article Title: Two tankers with 22 Indians on board hijacked by armed pirates off Yemen, Somalia
Article Text:
(Representative image): The pirates, suspected of being involved in a previous hijacking, reportedly steered the vessel towards Somalia's Nugaal coast.

Tanker with 16 Indians hijacked off Yemen

M/V LUTUF seized off Somalia

Indian seafarers face heightened regional risks

Two commercial vessels carrying 22 Indian crew members have been hijacked by armed pirates in separate incidents off Yemen and Somalia this week, with the sailors reported safe so far, according to a senior shipping ministry official. The Eritrea-flagged MT Sibu 1, carrying 16 Indians among 20 crew members, was seized in the Gulf of Aden on August 20, around 30 nautical miles off Yemen, while the Cameroon-flagged M/V LUTUF, with six Indians among its 10-member crew, was hijacked off Somalia's Puntland coast on August 17.The MT Sibu 1 was taken over by six armed pirates after an unauthorised vessel approached the tanker, while eight armed pirates operating from two skiffs boarded the M/V LUTUF off Puntland. Both vessels remain under pirate control, while no injuries have been reported among the crew.The Eritrea-flagged oil products tanker MT Sibu 1 was hijacked in the Gulf of Aden on August 20, about 30 nautical miles off the Yemeni coast. It was carrying 20 crew members, including 16 Indians, one Syrian, one Sudanese and one Iraqi national, while the nationality of another crew member is yet to be confirmed.Maritime tracking information indicates that the tanker was approached by an unauthorised vessel before control of the ship was lost.The shipping ministry official said, "As reported by Recruitment and Placement Service Licence (RPSL) agency - S K S Krishi Marine Services (Opc) Private Limited, six armed pirates are presently onboard the vessel (M.T. Sibhu-1) and have taken control of the vessel."The RPSL agency has been advised to submit an incident report and subsequent periodic updates through the e-Navik online marine casualty reporting system.The Cameroon-flagged M/V LUTUF was hijacked on August 17, around 3½ nautical miles off Marraya in Somalia's Puntland region. The vessel had 10 crew members, including six Indians, one Turkish national, one Georgian national and two Serbian security guards.Eight armed pirates, reportedly carrying AK-47-type weapons and travelling in two skiffs, boarded the vessel. The crew initially took shelter in the citadel, but the pirates gained access and moved them to the bridge before taking control of the ship."The vessel is reported to have been boarded by eight pirates, armed with AK-47-type weapons and operating from two skiffs."The crew initially mustered in the citadel. However, the pirates gained access and subsequently brought them to the bridge. The vessel is currently under pirate control. No injuries have been reported thus far," he said.The hijackers, suspected of involvement in a previous hijacking, subsequently steered the vessel towards Somalia's Nugaal coast. The ship was carrying Turkish weapons, communications and satellite equipment bound for a Turkish military training facility in Mogadishu.The twin hijackings come amid renewed security concerns for commercial shipping in the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and wider Indian Ocean. Vessels in the region have faced both piracy threats and attacks linked to the conflict in Yemen.The Forward Seamen's Union of India (FSUI) separately raised concerns over the "dangers faced by Indian seafarers amid the Iran war" and shared footage it claimed showed a vessel carrying 22 crew members, including 21 Indians, being hijacked in the Strait of Hormuz on April 22. It was unclear whether the footage related to a separate incident or the latest hijackings.India is the world's second-largest supplier of seafarers after the Philippines. The 2026 BIMCO-ICS Seafarer Workforce Report estimates that India supplies 311,936 seafarers, underscoring the scale of the country's exposure to maritime security threats worldwide.
Article Summary: Tanker with 16 indians hijacked off yemen; m/v lutuf seized off somalia. Both vessels remain under pirate control, while no injuries have been reported among the crew. India is the world's second-largest supplier of seafarers after the philippines.

Article Title: 'Proportionate response': MEA on bulldozer action outside Pakistan high commission
Article Text:
Debris lies scattered after authorities removed structures and queue-management barriers erected outside of the Pakistan High Commission, in New Delhi.

NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Friday said the removal of unauthorised structures outside the Pakistan High Commission in Delhi was a "proportionate action in response" to Pakistan's removal of structures in front of the Indian High Commission despite India's request not to do so.During the bi-weekly press briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said authorities had removed temporary structures in the lane of the Pakistani High Commission.“In Pakistan, some of the structures in front of the Indian High Commission were removed to facilitate parking. Despite our request not to do so, they went ahead with the removal," Jaiswal said."We then took proportionate action in response. There were some temporary structures in the lane of the Pakistani High Commission, which we removed," he added.On Thursday, authorities also removed traffic bollards and barricades that had previously been placed around the diplomatic compound.Visuals showed rubble outside the mission following the demolition, with broken metal railings and gates, twisted metal frames, roofing sheets, bricks, and chunks of concrete and plaster scattered across the paved area.The visuals also showed sections of the outer structures completely demolished, including corrugated roofing and white metal fencing.The visa section remained visible amid the debris, with service windows marked "Window 1", "Pakistani Passport Only" and "Window-5 / Collection of Visa Applications".The area around the service windows appeared damaged, with portions of plaster and masonry broken away.Broken fencing and construction material were also seen lying around the counters.
Article Summary: Mea: removal of unauthorised structures outside pakistan high commission in delhi was a "proportionate action in response" pakistan removed structures in front of indian high commission despite india's request not to do so. NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Friday hit back at the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom after it urged Washington to impose sanctions on members of Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh , calling the body "biased" and lacking credibility.In a bi-weekly press briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said such organisations have no credibility and operate to peddle their own agenda."The organisation you are talking about is known to everyone as a biased organisation, and for many years, it has been making misleading and provocative statements about India," Jaiswal said."I would say that we should stay away from such organisations because they peddle their own agenda and, at the same time, have no credibility," he added.This comes days after USCIRF urged the US government to impose sanctions on RSS members, rather than honouring them with "high-level meetings."In a post on X, the commission shared remarks from Asif Mahmood, a Pakistani-American physician who serves as its chair, and Commissioner Gene Mills.Mahmood described the RSS, the ideological parent of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), as an umbrella organisation, alleging that its affiliated groups had carried out attacks on religious minorities.Mills, meanwhile, said RSS leaders, even when affiliated with the Indian government, should not be given high-level meetings or diplomatic courtesies. NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Friday refused to interfere with criminal defamation proceedings against Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) president and former Punjab deputy chief minister Sukhbir Singh Badal over alleged remarks linking religious organisation Akhand Kirtani Jatha (AKJ) with banned terrorist outfit Babbar Khalsa International (BKI).A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu dismissed Badal’s challenge. Article Title: PLP to PLI, reform express at full speed, says PM Modi
Article Text:
PM Modi addresses ET World Leader Forum

Here's what PM said

Policies should be tailored for country, not country for policies: Modi

NEW DELHI: PM Narendra Modi said the country has moved from "production-linked punishment" (PLP), where companies were penalised for producing more by the "licence raj govts", to a regime where higher production is incentivised through schemes such as PLI (I for incentive), and vowed to pursue reforms with greater vigour to realise the goal of 'Viksit Bharat'."Our govt will continue working for the youth, women, farmers, the poor and the middle class. Our reform express will move forward at an even greater speed," he said at Economic Times World Leaders Forum on Friday.Amid growing global challenges, PM said, the world was seeing India as a "bright spot", where poverty levels have fallen, and with International Monetary Fund forecasting it as the fastest-growing major economy. A developed India will provide stability to a world ridden with distrust, where resources are being weaponised, he said. "For me, if India's future is secured, it will play a major role in bringing stability to the future of the world. "Slamming Congress-led opposition for mocking Atmanirbhar Bharat initiatives, Modi said they wanted people to remain helpless.A distorted mentality was at work behind such “production-linked punishment” (PLP) policies.People with that mindset always wanted a shortage of essential goods to persist. Their policy was to keep citizens in a state of scarcity, so that people would remain dependent on them. Their style of governance was to first make people plead before them and then act as if they were granting favours… You can imagine how such an approach strangled the basic principle of employment generation. What is even more surprising is that the courtiers of those govts — I repeat, their courtiers — never raised their voices against it, PM Narendra Modi said at ET World Leaders Forum Friday. He said, in contrast, production-linked incentive (PLI) has generated massive investments, created lakhs of jobs and helped boost exports.Modi said his govt’s approach was never to chase headlines or merely make pre-poll announcements that were never followed up. Instead of announcing free power, he said, NDA opted for the rooftop solar scheme that not only ensured reliable supply of electricity but also allowed individuals to supply to the grid and earn.“Today, we are making policies that are pro-people, pro-growth and pro-development. Policies should be made according to the needs of the country and its people. The country should not be forced to function according to policies.” He pointed out how elimination of railway crossings and interlocking have helped slash the number of rail accidents by over 90% to 15-20 annually. “Governance reform also means building systems that are sensitive to every human life and to people’s time. ”Modi highlighted Delhi-Meerut Namo Bharat Rapid Rail and Delhi Metro’s 99.9% punctuality record as a reflection of a change in mindset. “Earlier, if something was delayed, people would simply say, ‘this is Indian time’. Times have changed… Delhi Metro’s punctuality is now almost on a par with metro systems in cities such as New York, Hong Kong and Paris. This is not merely the story of metros and rapid rail running on time. It is the identity of an India that is changing with time.”Citing technological advancements that have made the average Indian’s life easier — from DigiYatra and FasTag to UPI payments and easier I-T return filing — PM said, “The ease-of-living reforms India has undertaken over the past 10-12 years have changed the lives of people, particularly the middle class, in ways that remain a dream even in many developed countries.”Ease of business has improved with compliance burden being lightened, he said, pointing out that outdated laws and compliance requirements have been done away with. Deregulation and reforms have had a major impact in crucial sectors such as drones, geo-spatial mapping, defence production and nuclear energy, he said.In his special address, Times Internet chairman Satyan Gajwani said Modi is now the longest-serving democratically elected head of govt among G7 and G20 nations. “Stable, long-serving leaders who are able to repeatedly win the trust of their voters do something for a nation. They infuse a nation’s soul with a sense of unity, security and confidence. That no matter what the challenge is, we will deal with it together. And we are in good hands. That we shall overcome. That sense of security and confidence then turns into magical things,” he said.“…A nation’s energy, self-belief, the dreams of its youth, the audacity of its entrepreneurs, the resilience of its farmers and, indeed, its destiny — all essentially flow from stable, long-term leadership,” he added.
Article Summary: Pm narendra modi said the country has moved from "production-linked punishment" (plp) to a regime where higher production is incentivised. He vowed to pursue reforms with greater vigour to realise the goal of 'viksit bharat' a developed india will provide stability to a world ridden with distrust, he said.

Article Title: 'World looking at India as bright spot of growth & hope': PM Modi at Economic Times World Leaders Forum 2026
Article Text:
From 'production-linked punishment' to PLI

'Prohibited unless permitted' to 'permitted unless prohibited'

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday said the world is looking at India as a "bright spot of growth and hope", stressing that the country's reform journey has shifted from a "punishment model" under the earlier licence raj governments to an incentive-based approach.Addressing the Economic Times World Leaders Forum 2026, PM Modi said the world had witnessed several ups and downs in recent years and that the future of all nations was interconnected."The world has witnessed many ups and downs over the past few years, and these experiences have made one thing abundantly clear: whether one likes it or not, the futures of all nations are interconnected. Nothing is possible in isolation," the Prime Minister said."'One Earth, One Family, One Future' was India's guiding mantra during its G20 presidency. This spirit of a shared future, along with the accompanying sense of responsibility, offers solutions to many of the challenges facing the 21st-century world. There are various concerns regarding global growth. The world has witnessed a grim scenario recently; resources are being weaponized, and an atmosphere of mistrust is giving rise to numerous new challenges.Yet, even in such times, the world views India as a bright spot of growth and hope," he added.PM Modi criticised the earlier licence raj governments, saying they followed a "Production Linked Punishment" (PLP) model that penalised companies for increasing production.“Today’s younger generation will be surprised to hear that there was a time in our country when if a company produced more than the prescribed limit, it was punished. This was the PLP, or Production Linked Punishment, model of the earlier licence raj governments,” he said.“Those who make fun of the Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat campaigns today are rooted in the same thinking of the past — PLP, or Production Linked Punishment,” he said.PM Modi also said the government is changing the country's regulatory philosophy by moving away from the earlier approach of requiring permission for activities unless explicitly allowed.“Earlier, the approach to regulations was ‘prohibited unless permitted’ — meaning you could not do something unless the government gave you permission. We are changing this approach to ‘permitted unless prohibited’. That means, for anything that is not explicitly prohibited by law, there should be no need to seek permission at every step.”He said the shift was intended to recast the relationship between the state, citizens and businesses around trust rather than suspicion.“The relationship between the government and citizens should be based not on suspicion, but on trust,” PM Modi added.The Prime Minister also highlighted legislative work undertaken during the Monsoon Session of Parliament."In the Monsoon Session of Parliament, we have passed the Bankers’ Books Evidence Bill, even as the Opposition has continued to create disruptions in Parliament. We did not allow the work of serving the country to stop," he said."We are not just changing regulations, we are changing entire policy of regulations," PM Modi said at the ET Global Leaders' Forum.Speaking ahead of PM Modi's keynote address at the summit, Times Internet chairman Satyan Gajwani said Modi had emerged as a source of stability in a world "lurching from one crisis to the next."Gajwani said the global landscape was being reshaped by multiple, overlapping disruptions - two ongoing wars, an energy crisis, disrupted shipping routes, trade wars and the rapid AI revolution - creating unprecedented uncertainty for governments, businesses and economies.He said India's political and economic stability, coupled with its growth and reform trajectory, had positioned the country as a reliable force amid growing geopolitical uncertainty.Gajwani said PM Modi's leadership and policy continuity had helped provide businesses and investors with greater predictability, while giving India an opportunity to play a larger role in the evolving global order.
Article Summary: From 'production-linked punishment' to pli - prime minister narendra modi. India's reform journey has shifted from a "punishment model" under the earlier licence raj governments to an incentive-based approach. Pm modi said the world is looking at india as a "bright spot of growth and hope"

Article Title: Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir sworn in as Bangladesh's 23rd President
Article Text:
Alamgir visited the graves of BNP founder Ziaur Rahman and former PM Khaleda Zia before the ceremony. He has been a close political ally of Khaleda Zia, the former BNP chief.

Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir was sworn in as Bangladesh’s 23rd President on Friday, taking charge as the country’s head of state after defeating his lone rival in the first contested presidential election in 35 years.The 78-year-old veteran politician and longtime secretary general of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) took the oath at Bangabhaban, the official office-cum-residence of the President, where Jatiya Sangsad Acting Speaker Kayser Kamal administered the oath at a ceremony attended by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, Opposition Leader Shafiqur Rahman, former Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus, Cabinet ministers, senior military officials and other dignitaries.Alamgir’s swearing-in came a day after he secured 255 votes against 88 for Colonel (retd) Oli Ahmed, the candidate of the Jamaat-e-Islami-led 11-party opposition alliance. His victory marked the first contested presidential election in Bangladesh since 1991, ending decades in which the largely ceremonial post was filled through consensus or uncontested elections.Ahead of the ceremony, Alamgir visited the graves of BNP founder Ziaur Rahman and former prime minister Khaleda Zia, where he offered prayers.He has been a close political ally of Khaleda Zia, the former BNP chief.Alamgir’s elevation to the presidency comes after a long career in Bangladesh politics, during which he served as the BNP’s secretary general and emerged as one of the party’s most prominent leaders.His election was closely watched as a departure from the recent pattern of uncontested presidential selections in Bangladesh. The contest against Oli Ahmed gave voters a direct choice between candidates backed by the ruling BNP and the Jamaat-led opposition alliance.With his swearing-in, Alamgir now formally assumes the country’s highest constitutional office, succeeding as Bangladesh’s 23rd President.
Article Summary: Mirza fakhrul islam alamgir was sworn in as bangladesh’s 23rd president on friday. The 78-year-old veteran politician and longtime secretary general of the ruling bangladesh nationalist party (bnp) took the oath at bangabhaban, the official office-cum-residence of the president.

Gisele Bündchen’s divorce from Tom Brady is no longer breaking news, but a deeply emotional 2024 interview still offers a revealing look at what the supermodel went through after their marriage ended. During a conversation with ABC News’ Robin Roberts, Bündchen struggled to hold back tears while reflecting on the end of a 13-year marriage, her children and the new chapter she was trying to build.The interview, released in March 2024 as part of “IMPACT x Nightline: Gisele Bündchen: Climbing the Mountain,” came more than a year after Bündchen and Brady finalized their divorce in October 2022.Their split ended a relationship that had lasted 16 years and a marriage that had lasted 13. By the time Bündchen sat down with Roberts, however, she was trying to understand the experience as part of a larger personal transition rather than simply an ending.Roberts reminded her that she had previously described the divorce as “the death of a dream.” The comment immediately struck an emotional chord.“Well, when you say ...” the model began, before pausing and getting teary. “Sorry, guys, I didn't know ... can I have a little moment?”After collecting herself, Bündchen spoke about accepting a future she had never expected to have.“It's definitely a time of, you know, a transition that had to take place, and it's not something that you — I don't think you wish for that, you know?” she said. “But I think sometimes in life things happen. I feel so blessed because, like, I wouldn't change anything in my life. I had incredible experiences. I learned so much. I have my children, which are the biggest blessings in my life.“And now I get to create — it's a new season, a new chapter in my life, and I get to learn new things, and I get to walk my path in a different way, you know?“And I'm grateful for all of it. I'm grateful for every lesson.”Her words showed that the divorce was not something she viewed in simple terms. There was pain, but there was also gratitude for the years she shared with Brady and the family they created.Bündchen and Brady share two children, Benjamin and Vivian. Brady also has a son, Jack, with actress Bridget Moynahan. For Bündchen, co-parenting meant accepting that the children would grow up moving between two different households and sets of rules.“There's easier days than others. But it's amazing that the kids — they're super smart children,” Bündchen said, laughing. “They know what they can get away with. So I think it's natural that it has different rules, and kids just adapt and they're going to try to do what they want. And I can only control what I do.”She also emphasized the value of her children having relationships with both parents.“It's amazing that they get to spend time with both parents because it's more enriching for their lives, two different worlds, and they get to learn from two different worlds.”Bündchen spoke warmly about Brady’s oldest son, Jack, whom she helped raise during her years with the former NFL star.“I raised him. I love him,” she said.Looking ahead, Bündchen said she wanted to live according to her own values rather than public expectations.“I'm very committed to living my truth more than ever, so I would say that's where my heart is now, where I am right now. I'm living my truth and I'm not apologizing for it,” she explained.The 2024 interview remains significant because it captured Bündchen at a vulnerable point in her life. She was not simply discussing a famous divorce. She was describing the difficult process of accepting change, protecting her children and finding an identity beyond a marriage that had once shaped so much of her public life.
Article Summary: Gisele bündchen and tom brady finalized their divorce in october 2022. The supermodel struggled to hold back tears while reflecting on the end of a 13-year marriage. She said she wanted to live according to her own values rather than public expectations.

A fan question on Kylie Kelce's podcast turned into one of her most honest moments yet. She views grief from pregnancy loss as something with no real end date, capable of resurfacing unexpectedly no matter how much time has passed or how many kids follow.It's a theme she's returned to more than once, and each time she's shared it, she's said the response from others tends to be more stories of loss rather than awkward silence.She was careful not to frame the fear as the end of the story, either. Article Title: Quote of the day by King Charles: "To my darling Mama, as you begin your last great journey to join my dear…" - a tribute to Queen Elizabeth, on gratitude, service and a son's farewell
Article Text:
Quote of the day by King Charles (AP photo)

Quote of the day by King Charles

"To my darling Mama, as you begin your last great journey to join my dear late Papa, I want simply to say this: Thank you. Thank you for your love and devotion to our family and to the family of nations you have served so diligently all these years. May flights of angels sing thee to thy rest"

What is the meaning of King Charles' quote

Why King Charles thanked Queen Elizabeth II

The personal meaning behind "my darling Mama"

What "the family of nations" actually means

Why Charles' farewell centred on service

The Shakespeare reference at the end of the speech

How the quote reflects the relationship between duty and family

How to apply the message in daily life

Some other memorable quotes by King Charles

"I am a dangerous person because I mind about things."

"It is important to be able to stand back and see the bigger picture."

"The environment is something that is very close to my heart."

"I think we have to be very careful about what we do to the natural world."

Few words spoken at a moment of personal loss carry the weight of an entire lifetime. When Queen Elizabeth II died on 8 September 2022, her eldest son, King Charles III, addressed the nation the following day, speaking as both a new monarch and a grieving son at the same time. Recorded in the Blue Drawing Room at Buckingham Palace, with a framed portrait of his mother resting on the desk beside him, his tribute combined personal affection, real gratitude and a recognition of her extraordinary decades of public service. It became one of the most widely remembered moments of that entire period, quoted on front pages across the country the following morning. For millions watching, the address offered a rare glimpse behind the crown, where duty and private grief briefly occupied space. His carefully chosen words also captured the enormous responsibility that had suddenly passed to him, making the moment deeply personal and historically significant.The speech also reassured a grieving public that the values associated with Elizabeth’s reign would continue, while Charles acknowledged the changes that lay ahead. His measured tone reflected both continuity and transition as Britain entered a new chapter.The address also marked the beginning of a new constitutional era, as Charles formally assumed the role his mother had held for seven decades. His message balanced continuity with change, reassuring the public while acknowledging the profound personal loss.At its heart, the message is about gratitude, love and farewell. Charles begins by describing his mother's death as a "last great journey," a gentle way of naming the end of a life, before referring directly to her reunion with her late husband, Prince Philip, who had died in April 2021. Rather than dwelling on the enormous constitutional change actually taking place, Charles places his mother's role firmly within a family context first. He thanks her for the love and devotion she gave to her family, before widening that same gratitude to the people and nations she served. The simplicity of the words "thank you," repeated before he expands on what he is actually grateful for, turns the tribute into an expression of appreciation for an entire lifetime of service.Queen Elizabeth II became monarch in 1952 and remained on the throne for more than seven decades, making her the longest-reigning monarch in British history. Across that period, she served under fifteen British prime ministers and witnessed enormous political, social and technological change. For Charles, though, her significance was never limited to her constitutional role alone. She was also, simply, his mother. His tribute moves between these two identities throughout, recognising her commitment to the "family of nations" she served while speaking about her in the deeply personal language of a son saying goodbye to his parent.The phrase "my darling Mama" gave the speech a genuinely intimate quality that stood apart from the formal language normally associated with royal addresses. Charles was speaking to a global audience, and yet the words themselves were directed towards one single person. Calling his mother "Mama" reflected the private family relationship sitting behind the public institution. Elizabeth II had been Queen to millions of people, but to her son she remained, simply, his mother. That contrast is really what gave the tribute its personal weight rather than letting it feel purely ceremonial.Charles' reference to the "family of nations" reflects Queen Elizabeth II's role across the Commonwealth, a voluntary association of independent countries, many with historical connections to the British Empire, of which she served as Head throughout her entire reign. Her role involved maintaining relationships with leaders and people across every member country, while representing a genuine continuity through decades of political change. Describing these countries as a "family of nations" highlighted exactly the relationships his mother had worked to maintain across the whole of her reign.A central theme running through Queen Elizabeth II's public life was duty. In her 1952 accession broadcast, she pledged her life to the service of the people of the United Kingdom and the Commonwealth. Seven decades later, Charles' farewell returned directly to that same idea. Describing her as having served "so diligently all these years" recognised both the length and the sheer consistency of that commitment. It also reflected the unusual nature of her reign specifically, since she continued carrying out official duties well into her nineties, including appointing Liz Truss as prime minister only two days before her death.Charles closed his tribute with the words "May flights of angels sing thee to thy rest." The line comes from William Shakespeare's Hamlet, Act 5, Scene 2, spoken by Horatio as he mourns his friend at the play's close, "Now cracks a noble heart. Good night, sweet prince, and flights of angels sing thee to thy rest." The reference gave Charles' speech a genuinely literary and solemn conclusion, connecting his personal farewell to one of the most recognisable expressions of grief in English literature, and its suggestion of a peaceful passage into rest made it particularly fitting for a speech delivered the day after losing a parent.One of the most powerful aspects of Charles' tribute is how it brings together two sides of Queen Elizabeth II's life at once, a mother within her own family, and a monarch with responsibilities reaching far beyond it. Charles' words acknowledge both directly, first thanking her for her "love and devotion to our family," then expanding that same gratitude outward to the people and nations she served. In the same speech, he also announced that Prince William and Catherine would become the new Prince and Princess of Wales, and expressed his love for Harry and Meghan "as they continue to build their lives overseas," a reminder that even a historic constitutional address remained, underneath it, a message about family.The circumstances behind this quote are genuinely unique, but its central message of gratitude applies just as well to ordinary relationships. Say thank you while you still can, since the people who matter most should never have to wait for a farewell to hear how much they are actually appreciated. Recognise quiet, unglamorous forms of service, since care and responsibility are often given without much recognition at all. Value family relationships alongside professional achievement, and remember that simple words of love and appreciation tend to become more meaningful, not less, with time.Why King Charles' farewell remains memorableCharles' first address as King carried an unavoidable constitutional significance, and yet its most memorable passage was deeply personal. He was not simply acknowledging the end of a historic reign. He was saying goodbye to the woman who had been his mother for more than seven decades. The repeated "thank you" captures the central emotion of the entire tribute. After a lifetime defined by public duty, Charles chose to close his first address as monarch with something considerably more private, a reminder that behind every title and institution sits an ordinary human relationship. A queen can be a constitutional figure to an entire nation while remaining, simply, "Mama" to her own son.
Article Summary: Quote of the day by king charles: "to my darling mama, as you begin your last great journey to join my dear late papa" queen elizabeth ii died on 8 september 2022, her eldest son, king charles iii, addressed the nation the following day. His tribute combined personal affection, real gratitude and a recognition of her extraordinary decades of public service.

Article Title: Dan Scavino, Natalie Harp, Walt Nauta: 3 aides were allowed with Trump when he was moved into a catering truck during Turkey emergency
Article Text:
Dan Scavino, Natalie Harp and Walt Nauta are the closest aides allowed inside the catering truck that hid President Donald Trump in Turkey.

Who is Dan Scavino?

Who is Natalie Harp?

Who is Walt Nauta?

No cabinet officials were allowed inside the catering truck, inside which President Donald Trump was snuck away last month in response to a potential Iranian assassination threat in Turkey. Apart from some low-ranking aides, only three individuals were allowed inside the truck, as they are believed to be the closest to the president: Dan Scavino, the White House deputy chief of staff; Natalie Harp, Trump's assistant and Walt Nauta, the director of Oval Office operations. Washington Post reported that neither Marco Rubio nor Pete Hegseth nor Stephen Miller were allowed inside the truck that took TrumpThe catering truck moved under concealment from the Air Force One aircraft to a smaller Air Force C-32A before flying to Britain separately.Dan Scavino has been serving as the White House deputy chief of staff in the second Trump administration but his history with Trump dates back to 1992, when he worked as a caddie at a New York country club that Trump later purchased and turned into Trump National Golf Club Westchester. After graduating from college, Scavino worked his way up to become the golf club's general manager.He joined Trump's 2016 presidential campaign and went on to serve throughout the entire first Trump administration as White House Director of Social Media and later Deputy Chief of Staff for Communications.During that time, he was particularly known for managing Trump's personal social media presence and online strategy. He remained a central advisor at Mar-a-Lago following the 2020 election, worked as a senior official on the 2024 campaign, and returned to senior White House leadership upon Trump taking office again in 2025.Natalie Harp is an American political aide and former television presenter who serves as Executive Assistant to the President in Donald Trump's second White House administration. She is the one who handles the president's daily schedule and is always spotted with him. Known colloquially among campaign staffers and media outlets as Trump's "human printer," Harp earned a reputation for constantly accompanying him with a portable printer to feed him printed news articles, polls, and favorable commentary. In her role as executive assistant, she remains a member of his inner circle, assisting with his daily schedule and managing dictation for his social media accounts.Walt Nauta is a close political aide to Donald Trump and currently serves in his second White House administration as Deputy Assistant to the President and Director of Oval Office Operations. Nauta spent 20 years in the U.S. Navy, reaching the rank of Senior Chief Petty Officer. During his military career, he was assigned to the Presidential Food Service and eventually became a White House valet during Trump's first presidency. In that role, he acted as a personal assistant and "body man," handling day-to-day tasks like fetching beverages and managing travel details.After Trump left office in 2021, Nauta retired from the Navy and joined Trump's personal staff at Mar-a-Lago, continuing to work as his primary executive assistant and political aide. He later drew widespread national attention when he was indicted alongside Trump in June 2023 in the federal classified documents case, where prosecutors accused him of helping move and conceal boxes of sensitive materials.
Article Summary: Dan scavino, natalie harp and walt nauta are the closest aides allowed inside the catering truck that hid president donald trump in turkey. They are believed to be the closest to the president and his inner circle. No cabinet officials were allowed in the truck.

Article Title: Thailand visit, Suu Kyi access: Can Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing win political legitimacy?
Article Text:
Min Aung Hlaing in Thailand; Aung San Suu Kyi with ICRC official

Min Aung Hlaing's ascent to power

Significance of Aung San Suu Kyi

Why Thailand visit matters for Min Aung Hlaing - and how Bangkok differs from ASEAN

Can regional engagement help Min Aung Hlaing’s legitimacy push?

Min Aung Hlaing’s continuing legitimacy challenge

Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing made a two-day state visit to Thailand last week, in a trip that carried significance beyond routine diplomacy. He remains internationally isolated because, in his earlier role as supreme commander of Myanmar’s armed forces, he led the 2021 coup that overthrew the elected civilian government. He subsequently ruled as head of the junta for five years before formally assuming the presidency.That visit to Thailand coincided with another significant development in Myanmar. Aung San Suu Kyi , the former leader whose government was ousted in that coup, was allowed to receive a visitor. On August 3, Suu Kyi met Arnaud de Baecque, the International Committee of the Red Cross' (ICRC) resident representative in her country.Naypyidaw also released photographs of the meeting—the first official images of the former State Counsellor in years.Was the close timing of the two developments just a coincidence? For Min Aung Hlaing, who came to power by overthrowing an elected government rather than through the ballot box, both developments could be part of a broader effort to build political legitimacy and gain wider international acceptance.During his visit to Thailand, the 70-year-old former military leader sought to reassure his host, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, that Myanmar was “returning to democracy.”"Myanmar has now re-established itself on the path to democracy and is moving toward a better future," Min Aung Hlaing told Charnvirakul.The remarks stood in sharp contrast to the circumstances of his rise to the presidency. His claim that Myanmar is on a “democratic path” also comes against the backdrop of a bloody civil war triggered by the coup that brought him to power.According to the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners, an independent organisation that documents arrests and casualties linked to the Myanmar civil war, more than 8,200 civilians had been killed and 31,645 people arrested by the regime's security forces as of August 5.Besides, the parliamentary elections under Min Aung Hlaing in late 2025 and early 2026 were also widely criticised as “neither free nor fair” as the army-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party swept the elections, winning 232 of the 263 contested seats in the lower house and 109 of 157 seats in the upper house. Ahead of the presidential election in April—Myanmar's first since 2018—he resigned from the military and was subsequently elected president.However, his transition to the presidency did little to ease international scepticism. Major democracies withheld congratulations following his victory.For Myanmar, Aung San Suu Kyi’s significance extends beyond her role as the head of the country’s first democratically elected civilian government in 50 years and the military’s toppling of her administration.For many inside and outside Myanmar, the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize laureate remains the country's most recognisable symbol of democratic rule and civilian legitimacy.In 2022, Suu Kyi was sentenced to 33 years in prison on a series of charges that her supporters and rights groups described as “politically motivated” and intended to prevent her return to politics. Later, her sentence was reduced to 27 years and, in April, to 18 years, while she was transferred to house arrest.Against this backdrop, the meeting with the ICRC representative was significant because it marked the first confirmed contact between Suu Kyi, 81, and an independent international organisation since her house arrest. It was also her first confirmed communication with the outside world since she wrote a letter to her son from prison in early 2024.Sreeparna Banerjee, an Associate Fellow at the Observer Research Foundation (ORF), agreed that both developments could be seen as part of Myanmar’s broader effort to “manage its international image,” but said it cannot be assumed that the moves were directly linked.“The timing is noteworthy, but it would be difficult to establish a direct connection between the two developments at this stage… Access to Aung San Suu Kyi after a prolonged period of isolation could signal some limited openness, while Min Aung Hlaing’s high-profile visit to Thailand demonstrates Myanmar’s attempt to expand diplomatic engagement,” Banerjee, whose work focuses on Myanmar and Thailand, told The Times of India.For Min Aung Hlaing, the bigger challenge remains turning such diplomatic engagement into wider political legitimacy and international acceptance.According to Banerjee, the visit was important for Min Aung Hlaing because it offered him a degree of political normalisation.“Being received at the highest level by an ASEAN neighbour allows him to project the image of a leader whose government is once again engaging with the region rather than remaining diplomatically isolated,” she said.Significantly, while Thailand and Myanmar are both ASEAN member states, Bangkok’s approach towards Naypyidaw differs from that of the rest of the 11-nation bloc of Southeast Asian states.Thailand has continued to engage with Myanmar despite ASEAN barring Min Aung Hlaing from its top-level meetings over the non-implementation of the Five-Point Consensus agreed with the grouping after he seized power.On this, Banerjee observed that the real value of Bangkok’s “bridge” diplomacy — acting as a bridge between Myanmar and ASEAN — would depend on whether Thailand can use it to encourage some meaningful progress on the Five-Point Consensus.Additionally, ASEAN is yet to recognise the results of Myanmar’s 2025–26 parliamentary elections. The bloc has also repeatedly called for Suu Kyi’s unconditional release, renewing the demand after her meeting with the ICRC official. The regime rebuffed this call too.For its part, Thailand has described its approach vis-à-vis Myanmar as one of “calibrated re-engagement” aimed at keeping dialogue open while responding to “realities on the ground.” Bangkok has also argued that Myanmar is essential to ASEAN unity and regional stability, provided it remains peaceful and stable.In addition to being barred from top-level ASEAN summits, Min Aung Hlaing faces Western sanctions over his role in toppling Suu Kyi’s government, the subsequent civil war, and the alleged persecution of the Rohingya minority in the Rakhine province.The Thailand visit was his fourth overseas trip since becoming president, following visits to India, China, and Laos. India was the only democratic country among the four destinations, underscoring the limited engagement he has so far had with democratic governments.Despite this, and close ties with Russia, he has remained largely isolated internationally.So, can his engagement with Thailand and his wider regional outreach — help him in his bid for greater international recognition and acceptance?Sreeparna Banerjee, the ORF Associate Fellow, suggested that even regional acceptance remains uncertain at this stage, despite such engagement being an important part of Myanmar’s quest for political legitimacy.“Naypyidaw appears determined to engage on its own terms rather than fully follow the ASEAN framework. Thailand's outreach may create space for dialogue, but whether this translates into wider regional acceptance remains uncertain,” she explained.She also highlighted that uncertainty over Myanmar’s regional acceptance stems in part from the fact that Singapore will take over the ASEAN chairmanship in 2027. The city-state has repeatedly called for full implementation of the Five-Point Consensus.This underscores the scale of the challenge facing Min Aung Hlaing in his bid for wider acceptance.For a leader who rises to power as Min Aung Hlaing did, securing international recognition is likely to remain a gradual and difficult process.The regime’s refusal to release Suu Kyi, a global icon, further complicates that effort.Engagement with neighbouring countries can provide an important opening, but broader recognition often depends on how other governments assess the resulting political situation. Yet for Min Aung Hlaing, this remains the only option to secure recognition.For now, engagement with Thailand may offer Min Aung Hlaing some diplomatic space, but whether it can translate into legitimacy for him remains uncertain.
Article Summary: Myanmar president min aung hlaing made a two-day state visit to thailand last week. He remains internationally isolated because, in his earlier role as supreme commander of myanmar’s armed forces, he led the 2021 coup that overthrew the elected civilian government.

Chamath Palihapitiya points to three things that are needed

Chamath Palihapitiya, a prominent venture capitalist and “All-In Podcast” co-host, has issued a warning to the leaders of top artificial intelligence (AI) labs, arguing that the technology sector is currently sitting on a dangerous ‘powder keg’ caused by mounting public and political opposition to physical data centres. According to Palihapitiya, the executive leadership leading cutting-edge AI development has failed to persuade citizens of the sector's merits and the community-level value of hosting infrastructure facilities.“Data centers have unfortunately become THE symbolic representation of the asymmetric upside for a very narrow tech elite and a class that are untrustworthy,” Palihapitiya said in a post on X (formerly Twitter).Palihapitiya’s remarks came as a direct reaction to reporting from Axios revealing that the campaign branch for Senate Republicans sent a stern memo to prominent AI development organizations. The communication from the National Republican Senatorial Committee pointed out that data centres have turned into a fierce campaign vulnerability in Ohio, where former Senator Sherrod Brown is competing in a tight race against Republican incumbent Senator Jon Husted.Husted is running to complete the remainder of Vice President JD Vance's term.“Texas, Pennsylvania and now Ohio. This is a powder keg and has the potential to unwind 200-300 basis points of annual GDP if it metastasizes. How did it get this bad? The collective leadership of frontier AI has failed miserably in doing the basics,” he added.The committee noted that the two candidates are locked in a dead heat, warning that data centers represent the heaviest anchor dragging down Husted's campaign.To repair the widening trust deficit, Palihapitiya advised industry figures to end internal conflicts and adopt an uplifting, accessible public message rather than relying on technical jargon or stoking doomsday scenarios.1. Paint a positive picture of what is possible with AI. Instead of spilling the ink on the glass half full, stories abound of pearl clutching, catastrophizing or arcane technical jargon that, together, breed mistrust, fear and skepticism.2. Visibly and disproportionately enrich the local communities AI data centers operate in. Tell these stories with a megaphone and have local leaders lead with the financial proof so it’s irrefutable.3. Stop infighting and stop trying to influence the government or trick them because of the asymmetric knowledge the industry has relative to outsiders and observers. This further makes it seem like a shady money grab to many bystanders.He stressed that companies must clearly demonstrate the positive everyday possibilities enabled by AI.
